# voprf_vx - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/voprf-vx/1.0.0-rc.0/voprf_vx/

## Expand description

An implementation of a verifiable oblivious pseudorandom function (VOPRF)

Note: This implementation is in sync with
[RFC 9497](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9497).

[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview

A verifiable oblivious pseudorandom function is a protocol that is evaluated between a client and a server. They must first agree on a finite cyclic group along with a point representation.

We will use the following choice in this example:

[§](https://docs.rs#modes-of-operation)Modes of Operation

VOPRF can be used in three modes:

- [Base Mode](https://docs.rs#base-mode), which corresponds to a normal OPRF evaluation with no support for the verification of the OPRF outputs
- [Verifiable Mode](https://docs.rs#verifiable-mode), which corresponds to an OPRF evaluation where the outputs can be verified against a server public key (VOPRF)
- [Partially Oblivious Verifiable Mode](https://docs.rs#metadata), which corresponds to a VOPRF, where a public input can be supplied to the PRF computation

In all of these modes, the protocol begins with a client blinding, followed by a server evaluation, and finishes with a client finalization and server evaluation.

[§](https://docs.rs#base-mode)Base Mode

In base mode, an [OprfClient](https://docs.rs/struct.OprfClient.html) interacts with an [OprfServer](https://docs.rs/struct.OprfServer.html) to compute the
output of the OPRF.

[§](https://docs.rs#server-setup)Server Setup

The protocol begins with a setup phase, in which the server must run
[OprfServer::new()](https://docs.rs/struct.OprfServer.html#method.new) to produce an instance of itself. This instance must be
persisted on the server and used for online client evaluations.

```
use rand::rngs::SysRng;
use rand::Rng;
use voprf_vx::OprfServer;
let mut server_rng = SysRng;
let server = OprfServer::<CipherSuite>::new(&mut server_rng);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#client-blinding)Client Blinding

In the first step, the client chooses an input, and runs [OprfClient::blind](https://docs.rs/struct.OprfClient.html#method.blind)
to produce an [OprfClientBlindResult](https://docs.rs/struct.OprfClientBlindResult.html), which consists of a [BlindedElement](https://docs.rs/struct.BlindedElement.html)
to be sent to the server and an [OprfClient](https://docs.rs/struct.OprfClient.html) which must be persisted on the
client for the final step of the VOPRF protocol.

```
use rand::rngs::SysRng;
use rand::Rng;
use voprf_vx::OprfClient;
let mut client_rng = SysRng;
let client_blind_result = OprfClient::<CipherSuite>::blind(b"input", &mut client_rng)
    .expect("Unable to construct client");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#server-blind-evaluation)Server Blind Evaluation

In the second step, the server takes as input the message from
[OprfClient::blind](https://docs.rs/struct.OprfClient.html#method.blind) (a [BlindedElement](https://docs.rs/struct.BlindedElement.html)), and runs
[OprfServer::blind_evaluate](https://docs.rs/struct.OprfServer.html#method.blind_evaluate) to produce [EvaluationElement](https://docs.rs/struct.EvaluationElement.html) to be sent to
the client.

`let server_evaluate_result = server.blind_evaluate(&client_blind_result.message);`[§](https://docs.rs#client-finalization)Client Finalization

In the final step on the client side, the client takes as input the message
from [OprfServer::evaluate](https://docs.rs/struct.OprfServer.html#method.evaluate) (an [EvaluationElement](https://docs.rs/struct.EvaluationElement.html)), and runs
[OprfClient::finalize](https://docs.rs/struct.OprfClient.html#method.finalize) to produce an output for the protocol.

```
let client_finalize_result = client_blind_result
    .state
    .finalize(b"input", &message)
    .expect("Unable to perform client finalization");
println!("VOPRF output: {:?}", client_finalize_result.to_vec());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#server-evaluation)Server Evaluation

Optionally, if the server has direct access to the PRF input, then it need
not perform the oblivious computation and can simply run
[OprfServer::evaluate](https://docs.rs/struct.OprfServer.html#method.evaluate) to generate an output which matches the output
produced by an execution of the oblivious protocol on the same input and
key.

```
let client_finalize_result = client_blind_result
    .state
    .finalize(b"input", &message)
    .expect("Unable to perform client finalization");
let server_evaluate_result = server
    .evaluate(b"input")
    .expect("Unable to perform the server evaluation");
assert_eq!(client_finalize_result, server_evaluate_result);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#verifiable-mode)Verifiable Mode

In verifiable mode, a [VoprfClient](https://docs.rs/struct.VoprfClient.html) interacts with a [VoprfServer](https://docs.rs/struct.VoprfServer.html) to
compute the output of the VOPRF. In order to verify the server’s
computation, the client checks a server-generated proof against the server’s
public key. If the proof fails to verify, then the client does not receive
an output.

In batch mode, a single proof can be used for multiple VOPRF evaluations.
See [the batching section](https://docs.rs#batching) for more details on how to perform
batch evaluations.

[§](https://docs.rs#server-setup-1)Server Setup

The protocol begins with a setup phase, in which the server must run
[VoprfServer::new()](https://docs.rs/struct.VoprfServer.html#method.new) to produce an instance of itself. This instance must be
persisted on the server and used for online client evaluations.

```
use rand::rngs::SysRng;
use rand::Rng;
use voprf_vx::VoprfServer;
let mut server_rng = SysRng;
let server = VoprfServer::<CipherSuite>::new(&mut server_rng).unwrap();
// To be sent to the client
println!("Server public key: {:?}", server.get_public_key());
```
The public key should be sent to the client, since the client will need it in the final step of the protocol in order to complete the evaluation of the VOPRF.

[§](https://docs.rs#client-blinding-1)Client Blinding

In the first step, the client chooses an input, and runs
[VoprfClient::blind](https://docs.rs/struct.VoprfClient.html#method.blind) to produce a [VoprfClientBlindResult](https://docs.rs/struct.VoprfClientBlindResult.html), which consists
of a [BlindedElement](https://docs.rs/struct.BlindedElement.html) to be sent to the server and a [VoprfClient](https://docs.rs/struct.VoprfClient.html) which
must be persisted on the client for the final step of the VOPRF protocol.

```
use rand::rngs::SysRng;
use rand::Rng;
use voprf_vx::VoprfClient;
let mut client_rng = SysRng;
let client_blind_result = VoprfClient::<CipherSuite>::blind(b"input", &mut client_rng)
    .expect("Unable to construct client");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#server-blind-evaluation-1)Server Blind Evaluation

In the second step, the server takes as input the message from
[VoprfClient::blind](https://docs.rs/struct.VoprfClient.html#method.blind) (a [BlindedElement](https://docs.rs/struct.BlindedElement.html)), and runs
[VoprfServer::blind_evaluate](https://docs.rs/struct.VoprfServer.html#method.blind_evaluate) to produce a [VoprfServerEvaluateResult](https://docs.rs/struct.VoprfServerEvaluateResult.html),
which consists of an [EvaluationElement](https://docs.rs/struct.EvaluationElement.html) to be sent to the client along with
a proof.

```
let VoprfServerEvaluateResult { message, proof } =
    server.blind_evaluate(&mut server_rng, &client_blind_result.message);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#client-finalization-1)Client Finalization

In the final step, the client takes as input the message from
[VoprfServer::blind_evaluate](https://docs.rs/struct.VoprfServer.html#method.blind_evaluate) (an [EvaluationElement](https://docs.rs/struct.EvaluationElement.html)), the proof, and the
server’s public key, and runs [VoprfClient::finalize](https://docs.rs/struct.VoprfClient.html#method.finalize) to produce an output
for the protocol.

```
let client_finalize_result = client_blind_result
    .state
    .finalize(
        b"input",
        &server_evaluate_result.message,
        &server_evaluate_result.proof,
        server.get_public_key(),
    )
    .expect("Unable to perform client finalization");
println!("VOPRF output: {:?}", client_finalize_result.to_vec());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#server-evaluation-1)Server Evaluation

Optionally, if the server has direct access to the PRF input, then it need
not perform the oblivious computation and can simply run
[VoprfServer::evaluate](https://docs.rs/struct.VoprfServer.html#method.evaluate) to generate an output which matches the output
produced by an execution of the oblivious protocol on the same input and
key.

```
let client_finalize_result = client_blind_result
    .state
    .finalize(
        b"input",
        &server_evaluate_result.message,
        &server_evaluate_result.proof,
        server.get_public_key(),
    )
    .expect("Unable to perform client finalization");
let server_evaluate_result = server
    .evaluate(b"input")
    .expect("Unable to perform the server evaluation");
assert_eq!(client_finalize_result, server_evaluate_result);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#advanced-usage)Advanced Usage

There are two additional (and optional) extensions to the core VOPRF protocol: support for batching of evaluations, and support for public metadata.

[§](https://docs.rs#batching)Batching

It is sometimes desirable to generate only a single, constant-size proof for
an unbounded number of VOPRF evaluations (on arbitrary inputs).
[VoprfClient](https://docs.rs/struct.VoprfClient.html) and [VoprfServer](https://docs.rs/struct.VoprfServer.html) support a batch API for handling this case.
In the following example, we show how to use the batch API to produce a
single proof for 10 parallel VOPRF evaluations.

First, the client produces 10 blindings, storing their resulting states and messages:

```
let mut client_rng = SysRng;
let mut client_states = vec![];
let mut client_messages = vec![];
for _ in 0..10 {
    let client_blind_result = VoprfClient::<CipherSuite>::blind(b"input", &mut client_rng)
        .expect("Unable to construct client");
    client_states.push(client_blind_result.state);
    client_messages.push(client_blind_result.message);
}
```
Next, the server calls the [VoprfServer::batch_blind_evaluate_prepare](https://docs.rs/struct.VoprfServer.html#method.batch_blind_evaluate_prepare) and
[VoprfServer::batch_blind_evaluate_finish](https://docs.rs/struct.VoprfServer.html#method.batch_blind_evaluate_finish) function on a set of client
messages, to produce a corresponding set of messages to be returned to the
client (returned in the same order), along with a single proof:

```
let mut server_rng = SysRng;
let prepared_evaluation_elements = server.batch_blind_evaluate_prepare(client_messages.iter());
let prepared_elements: Vec<_> = prepared_evaluation_elements.collect();
let VoprfServerBatchEvaluateFinishResult { messages, proof } = server
    .batch_blind_evaluate_finish(&mut server_rng, client_messages.iter(), &prepared_elements)
    .expect("Unable to perform server batch evaluate");
let messages: Vec<_> = messages.collect();
```
If `alloc` is available, `VoprfServer::batch_blind_evaluate` can be called
to avoid having to collect output manually:

```
let mut server_rng = SysRng;
let VoprfServerBatchEvaluateResult { messages, proof } = server
    .batch_blind_evaluate(&mut server_rng, &client_messages)
    .expect("Unable to perform server batch evaluate");
```
Then, the client calls [VoprfClient::batch_finalize](https://docs.rs/struct.VoprfClient.html#method.batch_finalize) on the client states
saved from the first step, along with the messages returned by the server,
along with the server’s proof, in order to produce a vector of outputs if
the proof verifies correctly.

```
let client_batch_finalize_result = VoprfClient::batch_finalize(
    &[b"input"; 10],
    &client_states,
    &messages,
    &proof,
    server.get_public_key(),
)
.expect("Unable to perform client batch finalization")
.collect::<Vec<_>>();
println!("VOPRF batch outputs: {:?}", client_batch_finalize_result);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#metadata)Metadata

The optional metadata parameter included in the POPRF mode allows clients and servers to cryptographically bind additional data to the VOPRF output. This metadata is known to both parties at the start of the protocol, and is inserted under the server’s blind evaluate step and the client’s finalize step. This metadata can be constructed with some type of higher-level domain separation to avoid cross-protocol attacks or related issues.

The API for POPRF mode is similar to VOPRF mode, except that a [PoprfServer](https://docs.rs/struct.PoprfServer.html)
and [PoprfClient](https://docs.rs/struct.PoprfClient.html) are used, and that each of the functions accept an
additional (and optional) info parameter which represents the public input.
See
[https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9497#name-poprf-public-input](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9497#name-poprf-public-input)
for more detailed information on how this public input should be used.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

-
The `alloc`feature requires Rust’s`alloc`crate and enables batching VOPRF evaluations.
-
The `serde`feature, enabled by default, provides convenience functions for serializing and deserializing with[serde](https://serde.rs/).
-
The `danger`feature, disabled by default, exposes functions for setting and getting internal values not available in the default API. These functions are intended for use in by higher-level cryptographic protocols that need access to these raw values and are able to perform the necessary validations on them (such as being valid group elements).
-
The `ristretto255-ciphersuite`features enables using`Ristretto255``CipherSuite`
-
The `ristretto255`feature enables using`Ristretto255`[Group](https://docs.rs/trait.Group.html)choice. To select a specific backend see the[curve25519-dalek](https://docs.rs/(https:/docs.rs/curve25519-dalek/4.0.0-pre.5/curve25519_dalek/index.html#backends))documentation.

# rmcp - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rmcp/2.1.0/rmcp/

## Expand description

The official Rust SDK for the [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25). Build MCP servers that expose tools, resources, and prompts to AI assistants — or build clients that connect to them.

For **getting started**, **usage guides**, and **full MCP feature documentation** (resources, prompts, sampling, roots, logging, completions, subscriptions, etc.), see the [main README](https://docs.rs/README.md).

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature Flags

| Feature | Description | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `server` | Server functionality and the tool system | ✅ |
| `client` | Client functionality | |
| `macros` | `#[tool]`/`#[prompt]`macros (re-exports)`rmcp-macros` | ✅ |
| `schemars` | JSON Schema generation for tool definitions | |
| `auth` | OAuth 2.0 authentication support | |
| `elicitation` | Elicitation support |

[§](https://docs.rs#transport-features)Transport features

| Feature | Description |
|---|---|
| `transport-io` | Server-side stdio transport |
| `transport-child-process` | Client-side stdio transport (spawns a child process) |
| `transport-async-rw` | Generic async read/write transport |
| `transport-streamable-http-client` | Streamable HTTP client (transport-agnostic) |
| `transport-streamable-http-client-reqwest` | Streamable HTTP client with default `reqwest`backend |
| `transport-streamable-http-server` | Streamable HTTP server transport |

[§](https://docs.rs#tls-backend-options-for-http-transports)TLS backend options (for HTTP transports)

| Feature | Description |
|---|---|
| `reqwest` | Uses rustls — pure Rust TLS (recommended default) |
| `reqwest-native-tls` | Uses platform-native TLS (OpenSSL / Secure Transport / SChannel) |
| `reqwest-tls-no-provider` | Uses rustls without a default crypto provider (bring your own) |

[§](https://docs.rs#transports)Transports

The transport layer is pluggable. Two built-in pairs cover the most common cases:

| Client | Server | |
|---|---|---|
| stdio | `TokioChildProcess` | `stdio` |
| Streamable HTTP | `StreamableHttpClientTransport` | `StreamableHttpService` |

Any type that implements the [ Transport](https://docs.rs/transport/trait.Transport.html) trait can be used. The

[helper trait provides automatic conversions from:](https://docs.rs/transport/trait.IntoTransport.html)

`IntoTransport`- `(Sink, Stream)`or a combined- `Sink + Stream`
- `(AsyncRead, AsyncWrite)`or a combined- `AsyncRead + AsyncWrite`
- A `Worker`
- A `Transport`

[§](https://docs.rs#license)License

This project is licensed under the terms specified in the repository’s [LICENSE](https://docs.rs/LICENSE) file.

# ferridriver_expect - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ferridriver-expect/0.5.0/ferridriver_expect/

## Expand description

Value matchers (Jest-compatible) and asymmetric matchers for
ferridriver’s `expect()` API. Shared between the test runner
(`ferridriver-test`) and the QuickJS scripting layer
(`ferridriver-script`) so both surfaces dispatch through the same
Rust core (per [the Rust-is-the-source-of-truth rule](https://github.com/salamaashoush/ferridriver/blob/main/CLAUDE.md)).

Web-first matchers (locator/page/apiResponse) still live in
`ferridriver-test::expect` because they need the test runner’s
polling + screenshot context. This crate is intentionally tiny:
`regex`, `serde`, `serde_json` deps only.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [api_](https://docs.rs/api_response/index.html)- response

- [asymmetric](https://docs.rs/asymmetric/index.html)
- Asymmetric matchers (`expect.any`,`expect.objectContaining`, …). Wire-encoded as a tagged JSON object so the script layer can produce them in JS and have them round-trip through`serde_json::Value`.

- `Expect<T>`builder shared by every consumer (test runner, QuickJS binding, plain Rust callers). Targets are subjects of web-first matchers —- `&Locator`,- `&Arc<Page>`,- `&HttpResponse`. Value matchers live on- `crate::ExpectValue`
- [diff](https://docs.rs/diff/index.html)
- Unified-diff rendering for assertion failures.
- [locator](https://docs.rs/locator/index.html)
- Locator web-first matchers — single source of truth shared by the
test runner (`ferridriver-test`) and the QuickJS binding (`ferridriver-script`). Screenshot / aria-snapshot / value-snapshot matchers stay in`ferridriver-test`because they pull in image and aria-YAML infrastructure that does not belong in this lightweight crate.
- [page](https://docs.rs/page/index.html)
- Page web-first matchers — url + title only. Snapshot/screenshot/
aria matchers live in `ferridriver-test`because they need the test-runner’s snapshot directory + image pipeline.
- [poll](https://docs.rs/poll/index.html)
- Generic async polling primitives shared by the test runner’s
`Expect<T>`and the script-layer`ExpectJs`binding.
- [throw](https://docs.rs/throw/index.html)
- Synchronous `toThrow`matcher (Jest’s`expect(fn).toThrow(...)`).
- [value](https://docs.rs/value/index.html)
- Synchronous value matchers (Jest-style).

# rmcp_macros - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rmcp-macros/2.1.0/rmcp_macros/

## Expand description

Procedural macros for the [RMCP](https://docs.rs/rmcp) SDK. Most users should depend on `rmcp` with the `macros` feature (enabled by default) rather than using this crate directly.

For **getting started** and **full MCP feature documentation**, see the [main README](https://docs.rs/README.md).

[§](https://docs.rs#available-macros)Available Macros

| Macro | Description |
|---|---|
| `#[tool]` | Mark a function as an MCP tool handler |
| `#[tool_router]` | Generate a tool router from an impl block (optional `server_handler`flag elides a separate`#[tool_handler]`block for tools-only servers) |
| `#[tool_handler]` | Generate `call_tool`and`list_tools`handler methods |
| `#[prompt]` | Mark a function as an MCP prompt handler |
| `#[prompt_router]` | Generate a prompt router from an impl block |
| `#[prompt_handler]` | Generate `get_prompt`and`list_prompts`handler methods |
| `#[task_handler]` | Wire up the task lifecycle on top of an `OperationProcessor` |

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-example)Quick Example

Tools-only server with a single `impl` block (`server_handler` expands `#[tool_handler]` in a second macro pass):

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use rmcp::{tool, tool_router};
#[derive(Clone)]
struct MyServer;
#[tool_router(server_handler)]
impl MyServer {
    #[tool(description = "Say hello")]
    async fn hello(&self) -> String {
        "Hello, world!".into()
    }
}
```
If you need custom `#[tool_handler(...)]` arguments (e.g. `instructions`, `name`, or stacked `#[prompt_handler]` on the same `impl ServerHandler`), use two blocks instead:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use rmcp::{tool, tool_router, tool_handler, ServerHandler};
#[derive(Clone)]
struct MyServer;
#[tool_router]
impl MyServer {
    #[tool(description = "Say hello")]
    async fn hello(&self) -> String {
        "Hello, world!".into()
    }
}
#[tool_handler]
impl ServerHandler for MyServer {}
```
See the [full documentation](https://docs.rs/rmcp-macros) for detailed usage of each macro.

[§](https://docs.rs#license)License

This project is licensed under the terms specified in the repository’s [LICENSE](https://docs.rs/LICENSE) file.

## Attribute Macros[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)

- [prompt](https://docs.rs/attr.prompt.html)
- prompt
- [prompt_](https://docs.rs/attr.prompt_handler.html)- handler
- prompt_handler
- [prompt_](https://docs.rs/attr.prompt_router.html)- router
- prompt_router
- [task_](https://docs.rs/attr.task_handler.html)- handler
- task_handler

- tool

# sidereon - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sidereon/0.10.1/sidereon/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#sidereon)sidereon

A thin, ergonomic API over the [ sidereon_core](https://docs.rs/sidereon-core/0.10.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/sidereon_core/index.html) engine. It does not model
anything itself: every function here delegates to a

`sidereon_core` reference
entry point and re-exports its result structs, so the numerical behavior is
identical to calling the core directly. The value it adds is a small, human
surface:- `load_sp3`
- `parse_antex`- `load_antex`
- `parse_rinex_nav`- `load_rinex_nav`
- `parse_rinex_obs`- `load_rinex_obs`
- `parse_rinex_clock`- `load_rinex_clock`
- `decode_crinex`- `load_crinex`
- `solve_spp`
- `solve_velocity`
- `solve_rtk_float_with`- `solve_rtk_fixed_with`
- `solve_ppp_float_with`- `solve_ppp_fixed_with`
- GNSS utility modules such as `frequencies``combinations``quality``carrier_phase``signal``velocity``broadcast_comparison``constants``navigation``geometry``data``dgnss``constellation``ppp_corrections``rtk``staleness``tides``ils``terrain`
- `astro`
- `tle`- `sgp4`- `passes`- `tca`
- one `Error`

The input, result, and ephemeris types each function takes and returns are
re-exported from `sidereon_core` under [ antex](https://docs.rs/antex/index.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/rinex/index.html)

`rinex`[,](https://docs.rs/astro/index.html)

`astro`[,](https://docs.rs/ephemeris/index.html)

`ephemeris`[,](https://docs.rs/positioning/index.html)

`positioning`[, and the curated](https://docs.rs/observables/index.html)

`observables`[/](https://docs.rs/rtk_filter/index.html)

`rtk_filter`[facades, so a consumer imports the ergonomic API types from this one crate. Lower-level RTK/PPP internals remain available under](https://docs.rs/precise_positioning/index.html)

`precise_positioning`[with their native core errors.](https://docs.rs/raw/index.html)

`raw````
// Malformed input surfaces a single error type.
let parsed = sidereon::load_sp3(b"not a valid sp3 file");
assert!(matches!(parsed, Err(sidereon::Error::Sp3(_))));
```
Lower-level helpers re-exported through modules such as [ rinex](https://docs.rs/rinex/index.html) keep their
native core error type. Map them explicitly at wrapper boundaries; there is
intentionally no blanket conversion into

[.](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html)

`Error`[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
fn decode_from_reexported_core() -> sidereon::Result<()> {
    sidereon::rinex::decode_crinex("not a CRINEX file\n")?;
    Ok(())
}
```
Low-level RTK and PPP core modules live behind the explicit [ raw](https://docs.rs/raw/index.html) escape
hatch, not the ergonomic facades.

`let _ = sidereon::raw::rtk_filter::RtkFilterScratch::new();`Hot-path RTK filter APIs are intentionally not part of the ergonomic
`sidereon::rtk_filter` facade.

PPP preparation and raw solver APIs are intentionally not part of the
ergonomic `sidereon::precise_positioning` facade.

RTK config builders consume the config. Dropping the returned value must not leave an unchanged copy available for solving.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use sidereon::{
    rtk_filter::{FloatSolveOpts, MeasModel, StochasticModel},
    RtkFloatConfig,
};
let epochs = Vec::new();
let ambiguity_ids = Vec::<String>::new();
let model = MeasModel {
    code_sigma_m: 0.3,
    phase_sigma_m: 0.003,
    sagnac: true,
    stochastic: StochasticModel::Rtklib,
};
let opts = FloatSolveOpts {
    position_tol_m: 1.0e-4,
    ambiguity_tol_m: 1.0e-4,
    max_iterations: 1,
};
let config = RtkFloatConfig::new(&epochs, [0.0; 3], &ambiguity_ids, &model, opts);
config.with_initial_baseline_m([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]);
let _ = sidereon::solve_rtk_float_with(config);
```
[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use std::collections::BTreeMap;
use sidereon::{
    rtk_filter::{
        AmbiguityScale, AmbiguitySet, FixedSolveOpts, FloatSolveOpts, MeasModel,
        ResidualValidationOpts, StochasticModel, ValidatedFixedSolveOpts,
    },
    RtkFixedConfig,
};
let epochs = Vec::new();
let ambiguity_ids = Vec::<String>::new();
let ambiguity_satellites = BTreeMap::new();
let wavelengths_m = BTreeMap::new();
let offsets_m = BTreeMap::new();
let float_only_systems = Vec::new();
let ambiguity_set = AmbiguitySet {
    ids: &ambiguity_ids,
    satellites: &ambiguity_satellites,
    scale: AmbiguityScale {
        wavelengths_m: &wavelengths_m,
        offsets_m: &offsets_m,
    },
    float_only_systems: &float_only_systems,
};
let model = MeasModel {
    code_sigma_m: 0.3,
    phase_sigma_m: 0.003,
    sagnac: true,
    stochastic: StochasticModel::Rtklib,
};
let opts = ValidatedFixedSolveOpts {
    float: FloatSolveOpts {
        position_tol_m: 1.0e-4,
        ambiguity_tol_m: 1.0e-4,
        max_iterations: 1,
    },
    fixed: FixedSolveOpts {
        position_tol_m: 1.0e-4,
        ambiguity_tol_m: 1.0e-4,
        max_iterations: 1,
        ratio_threshold: 3.0,
        partial_ambiguity_resolution: false,
        partial_min_ambiguities: 4,
    },
    residual: ResidualValidationOpts {
        threshold_sigma: None,
        max_exclusions: 0,
    },
};
let config = RtkFixedConfig::new(&epochs, [0.0; 3], ambiguity_set, &model, opts);
config.with_initial_baseline_m([1.0, 0.0, 0.0]);
let _ = sidereon::solve_rtk_fixed_with(config);
```

# sim_lib_plugin_core - Rust

## Expand description

Common plugin descriptors, state, and graph adapters.

```
use sim_lib_plugin_core::{
    ParameterDescriptor, PluginDescriptor, PluginFormat, PluginState,
};
let descriptor = PluginDescriptor::audio_effect(
    PluginFormat::Sim,
    "org.sim.doc-gain",
    "Doc Gain",
    2,
)
.unwrap()
.with_parameter(ParameterDescriptor::new(0, "gain", "Gain", 0.0, 2.0, 1.0).unwrap());
assert_eq!(descriptor.parameter(0).unwrap().plain_to_normalized(1.0), 0.5);
let mut state = PluginState::new();
state.set_param(0, 1.0);
let rebuilt = PluginState::from_expr(&state.to_expr()).unwrap();
assert_eq!(rebuilt.param(0), Some(1.0));
```

# log 0.4.33 - Docs.rs

# log

A Rust library providing a lightweight logging *facade*.

A logging facade provides a single logging API that abstracts over the actual logging implementation. Libraries can use the logging API provided by this crate, and the consumer of those libraries can choose the logging implementation that is most suitable for its use case.

## Minimum supported `rustc`

See the `rust-version` field in `Cargo.toml` for the current minimum Rust toolchain version.

This version is explicitly tested in CI and may be bumped in any release as needed. Maintaining compatibility with older compilers is a priority though, so the bar for bumping the minimum supported version is set very high. Any changes to the supported minimum version will be called out in the release notes.

## Usage

### In libraries

Libraries should link only to the `log` crate, and use the provided macros to
log whatever information will be useful to downstream consumers:

```
[]
 = "0.4"
```
```
use ;
```
### In executables

In order to produce log output, executables have to use a logger implementation compatible with the facade. There are many available implementations to choose from, here are some options:

- Simple minimal loggers:
- Complex configurable frameworks:
- Adaptors for other facilities:
- For WebAssembly binaries:
- For dynamic libraries:
- You may need to construct [an FFI-safe wrapper over](https://github.com/rust-lang/log/issues/421)to initialize in your libraries.`log`

- You may need to construct
- Utilities:

Executables should choose a logger implementation and initialize it early in the runtime of the program. Logger implementations will typically include a function to do this. Any log messages generated before the logger is initialized will be ignored.

The executable itself may use the `log` crate to log as well.

## Structured logging

If you enable the `kv` feature, you can associate structured data with your log records:

```
use ;
```

# log - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/log/0.4.33/target-redirect/log/

## Expand description

A lightweight logging facade.

The `log` crate provides a single logging API that abstracts over the
actual logging implementation. Libraries can use the logging API provided
by this crate, and the consumer of those libraries can choose the logging
implementation that is most suitable for its use case.

If no logging implementation is selected, the facade falls back to a “noop” implementation that ignores all log messages. The overhead in this case is very small - just an integer load, comparison and jump.

A log request consists of a *target*, a *level*, and a *body*. A target is a
string which defaults to the module path of the location of the log request,
though that default may be overridden. Logger implementations typically use
the target to filter requests based on some user configuration.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The basic use of the log crate is through the five logging macros: [ error!](https://docs.rs/macro.error.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/macro.warn.html)

`warn!`[,](https://docs.rs/macro.info.html)

`info!`[and](https://docs.rs/macro.debug.html)

`debug!`[where](https://docs.rs/macro.trace.html)

`trace!``error!` represents the highest-priority log messages
and `trace!` the lowest. The log messages are filtered by configuring
the log level to exclude messages with a lower priority.
Each of these macros accept format strings similarly to [.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/macro.println.html)

`println!`Avoid writing expressions with side-effects in log statements. They may not be evaluated.

[§](https://docs.rs#in-libraries)In libraries

Libraries should link only to the `log` crate, and use the provided
macros to log whatever information will be useful to downstream consumers.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use log::{info, warn};
pub fn shave_the_yak(yak: &mut Yak) {
    info!(target: "yak_events", "Commencing yak shaving for {yak:?}");
    loop {
        match find_a_razor() {
            Ok(razor) => {
                info!("Razor located: {razor}");
                yak.shave(razor);
                break;
            }
            Err(err) => {
                warn!("Unable to locate a razor: {err}, retrying");
            }
        }
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#in-executables)In executables

Executables should choose a logging implementation and initialize it early in the runtime of the program. Logging implementations will typically include a function to do this. Any log messages generated before the implementation is initialized will be ignored.

The executable itself may use the `log` crate to log as well.

[§](https://docs.rs#warning)Warning

The logging system may only be initialized once.

[§](https://docs.rs#structured-logging)Structured logging

If you enable the `kv` feature you can associate structured values
with your log records. If we take the example from before, we can include
some additional context besides what’s in the formatted message:

```
use log::{info, warn};
pub fn shave_the_yak(yak: &mut Yak) {
    info!(target: "yak_events", yak:serde; "Commencing yak shaving");
    loop {
        match find_a_razor() {
            Ok(razor) => {
                info!(razor; "Razor located");
                yak.shave(razor);
                break;
            }
            Err(e) => {
                warn!(e:err; "Unable to locate a razor, retrying");
            }
        }
    }
}
```
See the [ kv](https://docs.rs/kv/index.html) module documentation for more details.

[§](https://docs.rs#available-logging-implementations)Available logging implementations

In order to produce log output executables have to use a logger implementation compatible with the facade. There are many available implementations to choose from, here are some of the most popular ones:

- Simple minimal loggers:
- Complex configurable frameworks:
- Adaptors for other facilities:
- For WebAssembly binaries:
- For dynamic libraries:
- You may need to construct an FFI-safe wrapper over `log`to initialize in your libraries

- You may need to construct an FFI-safe wrapper over
- Utilities:

[§](https://docs.rs#implementing-a-logger)Implementing a Logger

Loggers implement the [ Log](https://docs.rs/trait.Log.html) trait. Here’s a very basic example that simply
logs all messages at the

[,](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Error`[or](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Warn`[levels to stdout:](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Info````
use log::{Record, Level, Metadata};
struct SimpleLogger;
impl log::Log for SimpleLogger {
    fn enabled(&self, metadata: &Metadata) -> bool {
        metadata.level() <= Level::Info
    }
    fn log(&self, record: &Record) {
        if self.enabled(record.metadata()) {
            println!("{} - {}", record.level(), record.args());
        }
    }
    fn flush(&self) {}
}
```
Loggers are installed by calling the [ set_logger](https://docs.rs/fn.set_logger.html) function. The maximum
log level also needs to be adjusted via the

[function. The logging facade uses this as an optimization to improve performance of log messages at levels that are disabled. It’s important to set it, as it defaults to](https://docs.rs/fn.set_max_level.html)

`set_max_level`[, so no log messages will ever be captured! In the case of our example logger, we’ll want to set the maximum log level to](https://docs.rs/enum.LevelFilter.html)

`Off`[, since we ignore any](https://docs.rs/enum.LevelFilter.html)

`Info`[or](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Debug`[level log messages. A logging implementation should provide a function that wraps a call to](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Trace`[and](https://docs.rs/fn.set_logger.html)

`set_logger`[, handling initialization of the logger:](https://docs.rs/fn.set_max_level.html)

`set_max_level````
use log::{SetLoggerError, LevelFilter};
static LOGGER: SimpleLogger = SimpleLogger;
pub fn init() -> Result<(), SetLoggerError> {
    log::set_logger(&LOGGER)
        .map(|()| log::set_max_level(LevelFilter::Info))
}
```
Implementations that adjust their configurations at runtime should take care to adjust the maximum log level as well.

[§](https://docs.rs#use-with-std)Use with `std`

`set_logger` requires you to provide a `&'static Log`, which can be hard to
obtain if your logger depends on some runtime configuration. The
`set_boxed_logger` function is available with the `std` Cargo feature. It is
identical to `set_logger` except that it takes a `Box<Log>` rather than a
`&'static Log`:

```
pub fn init() -> Result<(), SetLoggerError> {
    log::set_boxed_logger(Box::new(SimpleLogger))
        .map(|()| log::set_max_level(LevelFilter::Info))
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#compile-time-filters)Compile time filters

Log levels can be statically disabled at compile time by enabling one of these Cargo features:

- `max_level_off`
- `max_level_error`
- `max_level_warn`
- `max_level_info`
- `max_level_debug`
- `max_level_trace`

Log invocations at disabled levels will be skipped and will not even be present in the
resulting binary. These features control the value of the `STATIC_MAX_LEVEL` constant. The
logging macros check this value before logging a message. By default, no levels are disabled.

It is possible to override this level for release builds only with the following features:

- `release_max_level_off`
- `release_max_level_error`
- `release_max_level_warn`
- `release_max_level_info`
- `release_max_level_debug`
- `release_max_level_trace`

Libraries should avoid using the max level features because they’re global and can’t be changed once they’re set.

For example, a crate can disable trace level logs in debug builds and trace, debug, and info level logs in release builds with the following configuration:

```
[dependencies]
log = { version = "0.4", features = ["max_level_debug", "release_max_level_warn"] }
```
[§](https://docs.rs#crate-feature-flags)Crate Feature Flags

The following crate feature flags are available in addition to the filters. They are
configured in your `Cargo.toml`.

- `std`allows use of- `std`crate instead of the default- `core`. Enables using- `std::error`and- `set_boxed_logger`functionality.
- `serde`enables support for serialization and deserialization of- `Level`and- `LevelFilter`.

```
[dependencies]
log = { version = "0.4", features = ["std", "serde"] }
```
[§](https://docs.rs#version-compatibility)Version compatibility

The 0.3 and 0.4 versions of the `log` crate are almost entirely compatible. Log messages
made using `log` 0.3 will forward transparently to a logger implementation using `log` 0.4. Log
messages made using `log` 0.4 will forward to a logger implementation using `log` 0.3, but the
module path and file name information associated with the message will unfortunately be lost.

Libraries should link only to the `log` crate, and use the provided
macros to log whatever information will be useful to downstream consumers.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use log::{info, warn};
pub fn shave_the_yak(yak: &mut Yak) {
    info!(target: "yak_events", "Commencing yak shaving for {yak:?}");
    loop {
        match find_a_razor() {
            Ok(razor) => {
                info!("Razor located: {razor}");
                yak.shave(razor);
                break;
            }
            Err(err) => {
                warn!("Unable to locate a razor: {err}, retrying");
            }
        }
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#in-executables)In executables

Executables should choose a logging implementation and initialize it early in the runtime of the program. Logging implementations will typically include a function to do this. Any log messages generated before the implementation is initialized will be ignored.

The executable itself may use the `log` crate to log as well.

[§](https://docs.rs#warning)Warning

The logging system may only be initialized once.

[§](https://docs.rs#structured-logging)Structured logging

If you enable the `kv` feature you can associate structured values
with your log records. If we take the example from before, we can include
some additional context besides what’s in the formatted message:

```
use log::{info, warn};
pub fn shave_the_yak(yak: &mut Yak) {
    info!(target: "yak_events", yak:serde; "Commencing yak shaving");
    loop {
        match find_a_razor() {
            Ok(razor) => {
                info!(razor; "Razor located");
                yak.shave(razor);
                break;
            }
            Err(e) => {
                warn!(e:err; "Unable to locate a razor, retrying");
            }
        }
    }
}
```
See the [ kv](https://docs.rs/kv/index.html) module documentation for more details.

[§](https://docs.rs#available-logging-implementations)Available logging implementations

In order to produce log output executables have to use a logger implementation compatible with the facade. There are many available implementations to choose from, here are some of the most popular ones:

- Simple minimal loggers:
- Complex configurable frameworks:
- Adaptors for other facilities:
- For WebAssembly binaries:
- For dynamic libraries:
- You may need to construct an FFI-safe wrapper over `log`to initialize in your libraries

- You may need to construct an FFI-safe wrapper over
- Utilities:

[§](https://docs.rs#implementing-a-logger)Implementing a Logger

Loggers implement the [ Log](https://docs.rs/trait.Log.html) trait. Here’s a very basic example that simply
logs all messages at the

[,](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Error`[or](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Warn`[levels to stdout:](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Info````
use log::{Record, Level, Metadata};
struct SimpleLogger;
impl log::Log for SimpleLogger {
    fn enabled(&self, metadata: &Metadata) -> bool {
        metadata.level() <= Level::Info
    }
    fn log(&self, record: &Record) {
        if self.enabled(record.metadata()) {
            println!("{} - {}", record.level(), record.args());
        }
    }
    fn flush(&self) {}
}
```
Loggers are installed by calling the [ set_logger](https://docs.rs/fn.set_logger.html) function. The maximum
log level also needs to be adjusted via the

[function. The logging facade uses this as an optimization to improve performance of log messages at levels that are disabled. It’s important to set it, as it defaults to](https://docs.rs/fn.set_max_level.html)

`set_max_level`[, so no log messages will ever be captured! In the case of our example logger, we’ll want to set the maximum log level to](https://docs.rs/enum.LevelFilter.html)

`Off`[, since we ignore any](https://docs.rs/enum.LevelFilter.html)

`Info`[or](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Debug`[level log messages. A logging implementation should provide a function that wraps a call to](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Trace`[and](https://docs.rs/fn.set_logger.html)

`set_logger`[, handling initialization of the logger:](https://docs.rs/fn.set_max_level.html)

`set_max_level````
use log::{SetLoggerError, LevelFilter};
static LOGGER: SimpleLogger = SimpleLogger;
pub fn init() -> Result<(), SetLoggerError> {
    log::set_logger(&LOGGER)
        .map(|()| log::set_max_level(LevelFilter::Info))
}
```
Implementations that adjust their configurations at runtime should take care to adjust the maximum log level as well.

[§](https://docs.rs#use-with-std)Use with `std`

`set_logger` requires you to provide a `&'static Log`, which can be hard to
obtain if your logger depends on some runtime configuration. The
`set_boxed_logger` function is available with the `std` Cargo feature. It is
identical to `set_logger` except that it takes a `Box<Log>` rather than a
`&'static Log`:

```
pub fn init() -> Result<(), SetLoggerError> {
    log::set_boxed_logger(Box::new(SimpleLogger))
        .map(|()| log::set_max_level(LevelFilter::Info))
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#compile-time-filters)Compile time filters

Log levels can be statically disabled at compile time by enabling one of these Cargo features:

- `max_level_off`
- `max_level_error`
- `max_level_warn`
- `max_level_info`
- `max_level_debug`
- `max_level_trace`

Log invocations at disabled levels will be skipped and will not even be present in the
resulting binary. These features control the value of the `STATIC_MAX_LEVEL` constant. The
logging macros check this value before logging a message. By default, no levels are disabled.

It is possible to override this level for release builds only with the following features:

- `release_max_level_off`
- `release_max_level_error`
- `release_max_level_warn`
- `release_max_level_info`
- `release_max_level_debug`
- `release_max_level_trace`

Libraries should avoid using the max level features because they’re global and can’t be changed once they’re set.

For example, a crate can disable trace level logs in debug builds and trace, debug, and info level logs in release builds with the following configuration:

```
[dependencies]
log = { version = "0.4", features = ["max_level_debug", "release_max_level_warn"] }
```
[§](https://docs.rs#crate-feature-flags)Crate Feature Flags

The following crate feature flags are available in addition to the filters. They are
configured in your `Cargo.toml`.

- `std`allows use of- `std`crate instead of the default- `core`. Enables using- `std::error`and- `set_boxed_logger`functionality.
- `serde`enables support for serialization and deserialization of- `Level`and- `LevelFilter`.

```
[dependencies]
log = { version = "0.4", features = ["std", "serde"] }
```
[§](https://docs.rs#version-compatibility)Version compatibility

The 0.3 and 0.4 versions of the `log` crate are almost entirely compatible. Log messages
made using `log` 0.3 will forward transparently to a logger implementation using `log` 0.4. Log
messages made using `log` 0.4 will forward to a logger implementation using `log` 0.3, but the
module path and file name information associated with the message will unfortunately be lost.

# log/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)// Copyright 2015 The Rust Project Developers. See the COPYRIGHT
[2](https://docs.rs#2)// file at the top-level directory of this distribution and at

[6](https://docs.rs#6)// http://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0> or the MIT license
[7](https://docs.rs#7)// <LICENSE-MIT or http://opensource.org/licenses/MIT>, at your
[8](https://docs.rs#8)// option. This file may not be copied, modified, or distributed
[9](https://docs.rs#9)// except according to those terms.
[10](https://docs.rs#10)
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! A lightweight logging facade.
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//!
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//! The `log` crate provides a single logging API that abstracts over the
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! actual logging implementation. Libraries can use the logging API provided
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! by this crate, and the consumer of those libraries can choose the logging
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//! implementation that is most suitable for its use case.
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//!
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//! If no logging implementation is selected, the facade falls back to a "noop"
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//! implementation that ignores all log messages. The overhead in this case
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//! is very small - just an integer load, comparison and jump.
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//!
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//! A log request consists of a _target_, a _level_, and a _body_. A target is a
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//! string which defaults to the module path of the location of the log request,
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! though that default may be overridden. Logger implementations typically use
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//! the target to filter requests based on some user configuration.
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//!
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//! # Usage
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//!
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//! The basic use of the log crate is through the five logging macros: [`error!`],
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! [`warn!`], [`info!`], [`debug!`] and [`trace!`]
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//! where `error!` represents the highest-priority log messages
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//! and `trace!` the lowest. The log messages are filtered by configuring
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//! the log level to exclude messages with a lower priority.
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//! Each of these macros accept format strings similarly to [`println!`].
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//!
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//!
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//! [`error!`]: ./macro.error.html
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//! [`warn!`]: ./macro.warn.html
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//! [`info!`]: ./macro.info.html
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//! [`debug!`]: ./macro.debug.html
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//! [`trace!`]: ./macro.trace.html
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//! [`println!`]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/macro.println.html
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//!
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//! Avoid writing expressions with side-effects in log statements. They may not be evaluated.
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//!
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//! ## In libraries
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//!
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//! Libraries should link only to the `log` crate, and use the provided
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//! macros to log whatever information will be useful to downstream consumers.
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//!
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//! ### Examples
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//!
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//! ```
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//! # #[derive(Debug)] pub struct Yak(String);
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//! # impl Yak { fn shave(&mut self, _: u32) {} }

[60](https://docs.rs#60)//!     info!(target: "yak_events", "Commencing yak shaving for {yak:?}");
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//!
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//!     loop {

[64](https://docs.rs#64)//!             Ok(razor) => {

[66](https://docs.rs#66)//!                 yak.shave(razor);
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//!                 break;
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//!             }
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//!             Err(err) => {
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//!                 warn!("Unable to locate a razor: {err}, retrying");

[172](https://docs.rs#172)//! # Implementing a Logger
[173](https://docs.rs#173)//!
[174](https://docs.rs#174)//! Loggers implement the [`Log`] trait. Here's a very basic example that simply
[175](https://docs.rs#175)//! logs all messages at the [`Error`][level_link], [`Warn`][level_link] or
[176](https://docs.rs#176)//! [`Info`][level_link] levels to stdout:
[177](https://docs.rs#177)//!
[178](https://docs.rs#178)//! ```
[179](https://docs.rs#179)//! use log::{Record, Level, Metadata};
[180](https://docs.rs#180)//!
[181](https://docs.rs#181)//! struct SimpleLogger;
[182](https://docs.rs#182)//!
[183](https://docs.rs#183)//! impl log::Log for SimpleLogger {
[184](https://docs.rs#184)//!     fn enabled(&self, metadata: &Metadata) -> bool {
[185](https://docs.rs#185)//!         metadata.level() <= Level::Info
[186](https://docs.rs#186)//!     }
[187](https://docs.rs#187)//!
[188](https://docs.rs#188)//!     fn log(&self, record: &Record) {
[189](https://docs.rs#189)//!         if self.enabled(record.metadata()) {
[190](https://docs.rs#190)//!             println!("{} - {}", record.level(), record.args());
[191](https://docs.rs#191)//!         }
[192](https://docs.rs#192)//!     }
[193](https://docs.rs#193)//!
[194](https://docs.rs#194)//!     fn flush(&self) {}
[195](https://docs.rs#195)//! }
[196](https://docs.rs#196)//!
[197](https://docs.rs#197)//! # fn main() {}
[198](https://docs.rs#198)//! ```
[199](https://docs.rs#199)//!
[200](https://docs.rs#200)//! Loggers are installed by calling the [`set_logger`] function. The maximum
[201](https://docs.rs#201)//! log level also needs to be adjusted via the [`set_max_level`] function. The
[202](https://docs.rs#202)//! logging facade uses this as an optimization to improve performance of log
[203](https://docs.rs#203)//! messages at levels that are disabled. It's important to set it, as it
[204](https://docs.rs#204)//! defaults to [`Off`][filter_link], so no log messages will ever be captured!
[205](https://docs.rs#205)//! In the case of our example logger, we'll want to set the maximum log level
[206](https://docs.rs#206)//! to [`Info`][filter_link], since we ignore any [`Debug`][level_link] or
[207](https://docs.rs#207)//! [`Trace`][level_link] level log messages. A logging implementation should
[208](https://docs.rs#208)//! provide a function that wraps a call to [`set_logger`] and
[209](https://docs.rs#209)//! [`set_max_level`], handling initialization of the logger:
[210](https://docs.rs#210)//!
[211](https://docs.rs#211)//! ```
[212](https://docs.rs#212)//! # use log::{Level, Metadata};
[213](https://docs.rs#213)//! # struct SimpleLogger;
[214](https://docs.rs#214)//! # impl log::Log for SimpleLogger {
[215](https://docs.rs#215)//! #   fn enabled(&self, _: &Metadata) -> bool { false }
[216](https://docs.rs#216)//! #   fn log(&self, _: &log::Record) {}
[217](https://docs.rs#217)//! #   fn flush(&self) {}
[218](https://docs.rs#218)//! # }
[219](https://docs.rs#219)//! # fn main() {}
[220](https://docs.rs#220)//! use log::{SetLoggerError, LevelFilter};
[221](https://docs.rs#221)//!
[222](https://docs.rs#222)//! static LOGGER: SimpleLogger = SimpleLogger;
[223](https://docs.rs#223)//!
[224](https://docs.rs#224)//! pub fn init() -> Result<(), SetLoggerError> {
[225](https://docs.rs#225)//!     log::set_logger(&LOGGER)
[226](https://docs.rs#226)//!         .map(|()| log::set_max_level(LevelFilter::Info))
[227](https://docs.rs#227)//! }
[228](https://docs.rs#228)//! ```
[229](https://docs.rs#229)//!
[230](https://docs.rs#230)//! Implementations that adjust their configurations at runtime should take care
[231](https://docs.rs#231)//! to adjust the maximum log level as well.
[232](https://docs.rs#232)//!
[233](https://docs.rs#233)//! # Use with `std`
[234](https://docs.rs#234)//!
[235](https://docs.rs#235)//! `set_logger` requires you to provide a `&'static Log`, which can be hard to
[236](https://docs.rs#236)//! obtain if your logger depends on some runtime configuration. The
[237](https://docs.rs#237)//! `set_boxed_logger` function is available with the `std` Cargo feature. It is
[238](https://docs.rs#238)//! identical to `set_logger` except that it takes a `Box<Log>` rather than a
[239](https://docs.rs#239)//! `&'static Log`:
[240](https://docs.rs#240)//!
[241](https://docs.rs#241)//! ```
[242](https://docs.rs#242)//! # use log::{Level, LevelFilter, Log, SetLoggerError, Metadata};
[243](https://docs.rs#243)//! # struct SimpleLogger;
[244](https://docs.rs#244)//! # impl log::Log for SimpleLogger {
[245](https://docs.rs#245)//! #   fn enabled(&self, _: &Metadata) -> bool { false }
[246](https://docs.rs#246)//! #   fn log(&self, _: &log::Record) {}
[247](https://docs.rs#247)//! #   fn flush(&self) {}
[248](https://docs.rs#248)//! # }
[249](https://docs.rs#249)//! # fn main() {}
[250](https://docs.rs#250)//! # #[cfg(feature = "std")]
[251](https://docs.rs#251)//! pub fn init() -> Result<(), SetLoggerError> {
[252](https://docs.rs#252)//!     log::set_boxed_logger(Box::new(SimpleLogger))
[253](https://docs.rs#253)//!         .map(|()| log::set_max_level(LevelFilter::Info))
[254](https://docs.rs#254)//! }
[255](https://docs.rs#255)//! ```
[256](https://docs.rs#256)//!
[257](https://docs.rs#257)//! # Compile time filters
[258](https://docs.rs#258)//!
[259](https://docs.rs#259)//! Log levels can be statically disabled at compile time by enabling one of these Cargo features:
[260](https://docs.rs#260)//!
[261](https://docs.rs#261)//! * `max_level_off`
[262](https://docs.rs#262)//! * `max_level_error`
[263](https://docs.rs#263)//! * `max_level_warn`
[264](https://docs.rs#264)//! * `max_level_info`
[265](https://docs.rs#265)//! * `max_level_debug`
[266](https://docs.rs#266)//! * `max_level_trace`
[267](https://docs.rs#267)//!
[268](https://docs.rs#268)//! Log invocations at disabled levels will be skipped and will not even be present in the
[269](https://docs.rs#269)//! resulting binary. These features control the value of the `STATIC_MAX_LEVEL` constant. The
[270](https://docs.rs#270)//! logging macros check this value before logging a message. By default, no levels are disabled.
[271](https://docs.rs#271)//!
[272](https://docs.rs#272)//! It is possible to override this level for release builds only with the following features:
[273](https://docs.rs#273)//!
[274](https://docs.rs#274)//! * `release_max_level_off`
[275](https://docs.rs#275)//! * `release_max_level_error`
[276](https://docs.rs#276)//! * `release_max_level_warn`
[277](https://docs.rs#277)//! * `release_max_level_info`
[278](https://docs.rs#278)//! * `release_max_level_debug`
[279](https://docs.rs#279)//! * `release_max_level_trace`
[280](https://docs.rs#280)//!
[281](https://docs.rs#281)//! Libraries should avoid using the max level features because they're global and can't be changed
[282](https://docs.rs#282)//! once they're set.
[283](https://docs.rs#283)//!
[284](https://docs.rs#284)//! For example, a crate can disable trace level logs in debug builds and trace, debug, and info
[285](https://docs.rs#285)//! level logs in release builds with the following configuration:
[286](https://docs.rs#286)//!
[287](https://docs.rs#287)//! ```toml
[288](https://docs.rs#288)//! [dependencies]
[289](https://docs.rs#289)//! log = { version = "0.4", features = ["max_level_debug", "release_max_level_warn"] }
[290](https://docs.rs#290)//! ```
[291](https://docs.rs#291)//! # Crate Feature Flags
[292](https://docs.rs#292)//!
[293](https://docs.rs#293)//! The following crate feature flags are available in addition to the filters. They are
[294](https://docs.rs#294)//! configured in your `Cargo.toml`.
[295](https://docs.rs#295)//!
[296](https://docs.rs#296)//! * `std` allows use of `std` crate instead of the default `core`. Enables using `std::error` and
[297](https://docs.rs#297)//!   `set_boxed_logger` functionality.
[298](https://docs.rs#298)//! * `serde` enables support for serialization and deserialization of `Level` and `LevelFilter`.
[299](https://docs.rs#299)//!
[300](https://docs.rs#300)//! ```toml
[301](https://docs.rs#301)//! [dependencies]
[302](https://docs.rs#302)//! log = { version = "0.4", features = ["std", "serde"] }
[303](https://docs.rs#303)//! ```
[304](https://docs.rs#304)//!
[305](https://docs.rs#305)//! # Version compatibility
[306](https://docs.rs#306)//!
[307](https://docs.rs#307)//! The 0.3 and 0.4 versions of the `log` crate are almost entirely compatible. Log messages
[308](https://docs.rs#308)//! made using `log` 0.3 will forward transparently to a logger implementation using `log` 0.4. Log
[309](https://docs.rs#309)//! messages made using `log` 0.4 will forward to a logger implementation using `log` 0.3, but the
[310](https://docs.rs#310)//! module path and file name information associated with the message will unfortunately be lost.
[311](https://docs.rs#311)//!

[445](https://docs.rs#445)// The LOGGER static holds a pointer to the global logger. It is protected by
[446](https://docs.rs#446)// the STATE static which determines whether LOGGER has been initialized yet.
[447](https://docs.rs#447)static mut LOGGER: &dyn Log = &NopLogger;
[448](https://docs.rs#448)
[449](https://docs.rs#449)static STATE: AtomicUsize = AtomicUsize::new(0);
[450](https://docs.rs#450)
[451](https://docs.rs#451)// There are three different states that we care about: the logger's
[452](https://docs.rs#452)// uninitialized, the logger's initializing (set_logger's been called but
[453](https://docs.rs#453)// LOGGER hasn't actually been set yet), or the logger's active.
[454](https://docs.rs#454)const UNINITIALIZED: usize = 0;
[455](https://docs.rs#455)const INITIALIZING: usize = 1;
[456](https://docs.rs#456)const INITIALIZED: usize = 2;

[466](https://docs.rs#466)
[467](https://docs.rs#467)/// An enum representing the available verbosity levels of the logger.
[468](https://docs.rs#468)///
[469](https://docs.rs#469)/// Typical usage includes: checking if a certain `Level` is enabled with
[470](https://docs.rs#470)/// [`log_enabled!`](macro.log_enabled.html), specifying the `Level` of
[471](https://docs.rs#471)/// [`log!`](macro.log.html), and comparing a `Level` directly to a
[472](https://docs.rs#472)/// [`LevelFilter`](enum.LevelFilter.html).
[473](https://docs.rs#473)#[repr(usize)]
[474](https://docs.rs#474)#[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord, Debug, Hash)]
[475](https://docs.rs#475)pub enum Level {
[476](https://docs.rs#476)    /// The "error" level.
[477](https://docs.rs#477)    ///
[478](https://docs.rs#478)    /// Designates very serious errors.
[479](https://docs.rs#479)    // This way these line up with the discriminants for LevelFilter below
[480](https://docs.rs#480)    // This works because Rust treats field-less enums the same way as C does:
[481](https://docs.rs#481)    // https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/enumerations.html#custom-discriminant-values-for-field-less-enumerations
[482](https://docs.rs#482)    Error = 1,
[483](https://docs.rs#483)    /// The "warn" level.
[484](https://docs.rs#484)    ///
[485](https://docs.rs#485)    /// Designates hazardous situations.
[486](https://docs.rs#486)    Warn,
[487](https://docs.rs#487)    /// The "info" level.
[488](https://docs.rs#488)    ///
[489](https://docs.rs#489)    /// Designates useful information.
[490](https://docs.rs#490)    Info,
[491](https://docs.rs#491)    /// The "debug" level.
[492](https://docs.rs#492)    ///
[493](https://docs.rs#493)    /// Designates lower priority information.
[494](https://docs.rs#494)    Debug,
[495](https://docs.rs#495)    /// The "trace" level.
[496](https://docs.rs#496)    ///
[497](https://docs.rs#497)    /// Designates very low priority, often extremely verbose, information.
[498](https://docs.rs#498)    Trace,
[499](https://docs.rs#499)}
[500](https://docs.rs#500)
[501](https://docs.rs#501)impl PartialEq<LevelFilter> for Level {

[503](https://docs.rs#503)    fn eq(&self, other: &LevelFilter) -> bool {
[504](https://docs.rs#504)        *self as usize == *other as usize
[505](https://docs.rs#505)    }
[506](https://docs.rs#506)}
[507](https://docs.rs#507)
[508](https://docs.rs#508)impl PartialOrd<LevelFilter> for Level {
[509](https://docs.rs#509)    #[inline]
[510](https://docs.rs#510)    fn partial_cmp(&self, other: &LevelFilter) -> Option<cmp::Ordering> {
[511](https://docs.rs#511)        Some((*self as usize).cmp(&(*other as usize)))
[512](https://docs.rs#512)    }
[513](https://docs.rs#513)}
[514](https://docs.rs#514)
[515](https://docs.rs#515)impl FromStr for Level {
[516](https://docs.rs#516)    type Err = ParseLevelError;
[517](https://docs.rs#517)    fn from_str(level: &str) -> Result<Level, Self::Err> {
[518](https://docs.rs#518)        // iterate from 1, excluding "OFF"
[519](https://docs.rs#519)        for idx in 1..LOG_LEVEL_NAMES.len() {
[520](https://docs.rs#520)            if LOG_LEVEL_NAMES[idx].eq_ignore_ascii_case(level) {
[521](https://docs.rs#521)                return Ok(Level::from_usize(idx).unwrap());
[522](https://docs.rs#522)            }
[523](https://docs.rs#523)        }
[524](https://docs.rs#524)        Err(ParseLevelError(()))
[525](https://docs.rs#525)    }
[526](https://docs.rs#526)}

[530](https://docs.rs#530)        fmt.pad(self.as_str())
[531](https://docs.rs#531)    }

[534](https://docs.rs#534)impl Level {
[535](https://docs.rs#535)    fn from_usize(u: usize) -> Option<Level> {
[536](https://docs.rs#536)        match u {
[537](https://docs.rs#537)            1 => Some(Level::Error),
[538](https://docs.rs#538)            2 => Some(Level::Warn),
[539](https://docs.rs#539)            3 => Some(Level::Info),
[540](https://docs.rs#540)            4 => Some(Level::Debug),
[541](https://docs.rs#541)            5 => Some(Level::Trace),
[542](https://docs.rs#542)            _ => None,
[543](https://docs.rs#543)        }
[544](https://docs.rs#544)    }
[545](https://docs.rs#545)
[546](https://docs.rs#546)    /// Returns the most verbose logging level.
[547](https://docs.rs#547)    #[inline]
[548](https://docs.rs#548)    pub fn max() -> Level {
[549](https://docs.rs#549)        Level::Trace
[550](https://docs.rs#550)    }
[551](https://docs.rs#551)
[552](https://docs.rs#552)    /// Converts the `Level` to the equivalent `LevelFilter`.
[553](https://docs.rs#553)    #[inline]
[554](https://docs.rs#554)    pub fn to_level_filter(&self) -> LevelFilter {
[555](https://docs.rs#555)        LevelFilter::from_usize(*self as usize).unwrap()
[556](https://docs.rs#556)    }
[557](https://docs.rs#557)
[558](https://docs.rs#558)    /// Returns the string representation of the `Level`.
[559](https://docs.rs#559)    ///
[560](https://docs.rs#560)    /// This returns the same string as the `fmt::Display` implementation.
[561](https://docs.rs#561)    pub fn as_str(&self) -> &'static str {
[562](https://docs.rs#562)        LOG_LEVEL_NAMES[*self as usize]
[563](https://docs.rs#563)    }
[564](https://docs.rs#564)
[565](https://docs.rs#565)    /// Iterate through all supported logging levels.
[566](https://docs.rs#566)    ///
[567](https://docs.rs#567)    /// The order of iteration is from more severe to less severe log messages.
[568](https://docs.rs#568)    ///
[569](https://docs.rs#569)    /// # Examples
[570](https://docs.rs#570)    ///
[571](https://docs.rs#571)    /// ```
[572](https://docs.rs#572)    /// use log::Level;
[573](https://docs.rs#573)    ///
[574](https://docs.rs#574)    /// let mut levels = Level::iter();
[575](https://docs.rs#575)    ///
[576](https://docs.rs#576)    /// assert_eq!(Some(Level::Error), levels.next());
[577](https://docs.rs#577)    /// assert_eq!(Some(Level::Trace), levels.last());
[578](https://docs.rs#578)    /// ```
[579](https://docs.rs#579)    pub fn iter() -> impl Iterator<Item = Self> {
[580](https://docs.rs#580)        (1..6).map(|i| Self::from_usize(i).unwrap())
[581](https://docs.rs#581)    }
[582](https://docs.rs#582)
[583](https://docs.rs#583)    /// Get the next-highest `Level` from this one.
[584](https://docs.rs#584)    ///
[585](https://docs.rs#585)    /// If the current `Level` is at the highest level, the returned `Level` will be the same as the
[586](https://docs.rs#586)    /// current one.
[587](https://docs.rs#587)    ///
[588](https://docs.rs#588)    /// # Examples
[589](https://docs.rs#589)    ///
[590](https://docs.rs#590)    /// ```
[591](https://docs.rs#591)    /// use log::Level;
[592](https://docs.rs#592)    ///
[593](https://docs.rs#593)    /// let level = Level::Info;
[594](https://docs.rs#594)    ///
[595](https://docs.rs#595)    /// assert_eq!(Level::Debug, level.increment_severity());
[596](https://docs.rs#596)    /// assert_eq!(Level::Trace, level.increment_severity().increment_severity());
[597](https://docs.rs#597)    /// assert_eq!(Level::Trace, level.increment_severity().increment_severity().increment_severity()); // max level
[598](https://docs.rs#598)    /// ```
[599](https://docs.rs#599)    pub fn increment_severity(&self) -> Self {
[600](https://docs.rs#600)        let current = *self as usize;
[601](https://docs.rs#601)        Self::from_usize(current + 1).unwrap_or(*self)
[602](https://docs.rs#602)    }
[603](https://docs.rs#603)
[604](https://docs.rs#604)    /// Get the next-lowest `Level` from this one.
[605](https://docs.rs#605)    ///
[606](https://docs.rs#606)    /// If the current `Level` is at the lowest level, the returned `Level` will be the same as the
[607](https://docs.rs#607)    /// current one.
[608](https://docs.rs#608)    ///
[609](https://docs.rs#609)    /// # Examples
[610](https://docs.rs#610)    ///
[611](https://docs.rs#611)    /// ```
[612](https://docs.rs#612)    /// use log::Level;
[613](https://docs.rs#613)    ///
[614](https://docs.rs#614)    /// let level = Level::Info;
[615](https://docs.rs#615)    ///
[616](https://docs.rs#616)    /// assert_eq!(Level::Warn, level.decrement_severity());
[617](https://docs.rs#617)    /// assert_eq!(Level::Error, level.decrement_severity().decrement_severity());
[618](https://docs.rs#618)    /// assert_eq!(Level::Error, level.decrement_severity().decrement_severity().decrement_severity()); // min level
[619](https://docs.rs#619)    /// ```
[620](https://docs.rs#620)    pub fn decrement_severity(&self) -> Self {
[621](https://docs.rs#621)        let current = *self as usize;
[622](https://docs.rs#622)        Self::from_usize(current.saturating_sub(1)).unwrap_or(*self)
[623](https://docs.rs#623)    }

[626](https://docs.rs#626)/// An enum representing the available verbosity level filters of the logger.
[627](https://docs.rs#627)///
[628](https://docs.rs#628)/// A `LevelFilter` may be compared directly to a [`Level`]. Use this type
[629](https://docs.rs#629)/// to get and set the maximum log level with [`max_level()`] and [`set_max_level`].
[630](https://docs.rs#630)///
[631](https://docs.rs#631)/// [`Level`]: enum.Level.html
[632](https://docs.rs#632)/// [`max_level()`]: fn.max_level.html
[633](https://docs.rs#633)/// [`set_max_level`]: fn.set_max_level.html
[634](https://docs.rs#634)#[repr(usize)]

[636](https://docs.rs#636)pub enum LevelFilter {
[637](https://docs.rs#637)    /// A level lower than all log levels.
[638](https://docs.rs#638)    Off,
[639](https://docs.rs#639)    /// Corresponds to the `Error` log level.
[640](https://docs.rs#640)    Error,
[641](https://docs.rs#641)    /// Corresponds to the `Warn` log level.
[642](https://docs.rs#642)    Warn,
[643](https://docs.rs#643)    /// Corresponds to the `Info` log level.
[644](https://docs.rs#644)    Info,
[645](https://docs.rs#645)    /// Corresponds to the `Debug` log level.
[646](https://docs.rs#646)    Debug,
[647](https://docs.rs#647)    /// Corresponds to the `Trace` log level.
[648](https://docs.rs#648)    Trace,
[649](https://docs.rs#649)}
[650](https://docs.rs#650)

[655](https://docs.rs#655)    }

[662](https://docs.rs#662)    }

[665](https://docs.rs#665)impl FromStr for LevelFilter {
[666](https://docs.rs#666)    type Err = ParseLevelError;
[667](https://docs.rs#667)    fn from_str(level: &str) -> Result<LevelFilter, Self::Err> {
[668](https://docs.rs#668)        // iterate from 0, including "OFF"
[669](https://docs.rs#669)        for idx in 0..LOG_LEVEL_NAMES.len() {
[670](https://docs.rs#670)            if LOG_LEVEL_NAMES[idx].eq_ignore_ascii_case(level) {
[671](https://docs.rs#671)                return Ok(LevelFilter::from_usize(idx).unwrap());
[672](https://docs.rs#672)            }
[673](https://docs.rs#673)        }
[674](https://docs.rs#674)        Err(ParseLevelError(()))
[675](https://docs.rs#675)    }
[676](https://docs.rs#676)}

[822](https://docs.rs#822)/// The "payload" of a log message.
[823](https://docs.rs#823)///
[824](https://docs.rs#824)/// # Use
[825](https://docs.rs#825)///
[826](https://docs.rs#826)/// `Record` structures are passed as parameters to the [`log`][method.log]
[827](https://docs.rs#827)/// method of the [`Log`] trait. Logger implementors manipulate these
[828](https://docs.rs#828)/// structures in order to display log messages. `Record`s are automatically
[829](https://docs.rs#829)/// created by the [`log!`] macro and so are not seen by log users.
[830](https://docs.rs#830)///
[831](https://docs.rs#831)/// Note that the [`level()`] and [`target()`] accessors are equivalent to
[832](https://docs.rs#832)/// `self.metadata().level()` and `self.metadata().target()` respectively.
[833](https://docs.rs#833)/// These methods are provided as a convenience for users of this structure.
[834](https://docs.rs#834)///
[835](https://docs.rs#835)/// # Example
[836](https://docs.rs#836)///
[837](https://docs.rs#837)/// The following example shows a simple logger that displays the level,
[838](https://docs.rs#838)/// module path, and message of any `Record` that is passed to it.
[839](https://docs.rs#839)///
[840](https://docs.rs#840)/// ```
[841](https://docs.rs#841)/// struct SimpleLogger;
[842](https://docs.rs#842)///
[843](https://docs.rs#843)/// impl log::Log for SimpleLogger {
[844](https://docs.rs#844)///    fn enabled(&self, _metadata: &log::Metadata) -> bool {
[845](https://docs.rs#845)///        true
[846](https://docs.rs#846)///    }
[847](https://docs.rs#847)///
[848](https://docs.rs#848)///    fn log(&self, record: &log::Record) {
[849](https://docs.rs#849)///        if !self.enabled(record.metadata()) {
[850](https://docs.rs#850)///            return;
[851](https://docs.rs#851)///        }
[852](https://docs.rs#852)///
[853](https://docs.rs#853)///        println!("{}:{} -- {}",
[854](https://docs.rs#854)///                 record.level(),
[855](https://docs.rs#855)///                 record.target(),
[856](https://docs.rs#856)///                 record.args());
[857](https://docs.rs#857)///    }
[858](https://docs.rs#858)///    fn flush(&self) {}
[859](https://docs.rs#859)/// }
[860](https://docs.rs#860)/// ```
[861](https://docs.rs#861)///
[862](https://docs.rs#862)/// [method.log]: trait.Log.html#tymethod.log
[863](https://docs.rs#863)/// [`Log`]: trait.Log.html
[864](https://docs.rs#864)/// [`log!`]: macro.log.html
[865](https://docs.rs#865)/// [`level()`]: struct.Record.html#method.level
[866](https://docs.rs#866)/// [`target()`]: struct.Record.html#method.target
[867](https://docs.rs#867)#[derive(Clone, Debug)]
[868](https://docs.rs#868)pub struct Record<'a> {
[869](https://docs.rs#869)    metadata: Metadata<'a>,
[870](https://docs.rs#870)    args: fmt::Arguments<'a>,
[871](https://docs.rs#871)    module_path: Option<MaybeStaticStr<'a>>,
[872](https://docs.rs#872)    file: Option<MaybeStaticStr<'a>>,
[873](https://docs.rs#873)    line: Option<u32>,
[874](https://docs.rs#874)    #[cfg(feature = "kv")]
[875](https://docs.rs#875)    key_values: KeyValues<'a>,
[876](https://docs.rs#876)}
[877](https://docs.rs#877)
[878](https://docs.rs#878)// This wrapper type is only needed so we can
[879](https://docs.rs#879)// `#[derive(Debug)]` on `Record`. It also
[880](https://docs.rs#880)// provides a useful `Debug` implementation for
[881](https://docs.rs#881)// the underlying `Source`.
[882](https://docs.rs#882)#[cfg(feature = "kv")]
[883](https://docs.rs#883)#[derive(Clone)]
[884](https://docs.rs#884)struct KeyValues<'a>(&'a dyn kv::Source);
[885](https://docs.rs#885)
[886](https://docs.rs#886)#[cfg(feature = "kv")]
[887](https://docs.rs#887)impl<'a> fmt::Debug for KeyValues<'a> {
[888](https://docs.rs#888)    fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result {
[889](https://docs.rs#889)        let mut visitor = f.debug_map();
[890](https://docs.rs#890)        self.0.visit(&mut visitor).map_err(|_| fmt::Error)?;
[891](https://docs.rs#891)        visitor.finish()
[892](https://docs.rs#892)    }
[893](https://docs.rs#893)}

[988](https://docs.rs#988)
[989](https://docs.rs#989)/// Builder for [`Record`](struct.Record.html).
[990](https://docs.rs#990)///
[991](https://docs.rs#991)/// Typically should only be used by log library creators or for testing and "shim loggers".
[992](https://docs.rs#992)/// The `RecordBuilder` can set the different parameters of `Record` object, and returns
[993](https://docs.rs#993)/// the created object when `build` is called.
[994](https://docs.rs#994)///
[995](https://docs.rs#995)/// # Examples
[996](https://docs.rs#996)///
[997](https://docs.rs#997)/// ```
[998](https://docs.rs#998)/// use log::{Level, Record};
[999](https://docs.rs#999)///
[1000](https://docs.rs#1000)/// let record = Record::builder()
[1001](https://docs.rs#1001)///                 .args(format_args!("Error!"))
[1002](https://docs.rs#1002)///                 .level(Level::Error)
[1003](https://docs.rs#1003)///                 .target("myApp")
[1004](https://docs.rs#1004)///                 .file(Some("server.rs"))
[1005](https://docs.rs#1005)///                 .line(Some(144))
[1006](https://docs.rs#1006)///                 .module_path(Some("server"))
[1007](https://docs.rs#1007)///                 .build();
[1008](https://docs.rs#1008)/// ```
[1009](https://docs.rs#1009)///
[1010](https://docs.rs#1010)/// Alternatively, use [`MetadataBuilder`](struct.MetadataBuilder.html):
[1011](https://docs.rs#1011)///
[1012](https://docs.rs#1012)/// ```
[1013](https://docs.rs#1013)/// use log::{Record, Level, MetadataBuilder};
[1014](https://docs.rs#1014)///
[1015](https://docs.rs#1015)/// let error_metadata = MetadataBuilder::new()
[1016](https://docs.rs#1016)///                         .target("myApp")
[1017](https://docs.rs#1017)///                         .level(Level::Error)
[1018](https://docs.rs#1018)///                         .build();
[1019](https://docs.rs#1019)///
[1020](https://docs.rs#1020)/// let record = Record::builder()
[1021](https://docs.rs#1021)///                 .metadata(error_metadata)
[1022](https://docs.rs#1022)///                 .args(format_args!("Error!"))
[1023](https://docs.rs#1023)///                 .line(Some(433))
[1024](https://docs.rs#1024)///                 .file(Some("app.rs"))
[1025](https://docs.rs#1025)///                 .module_path(Some("server"))
[1026](https://docs.rs#1026)///                 .build();
[1027](https://docs.rs#1027)/// ```
[1028](https://docs.rs#1028)#[derive(Debug)]
[1029](https://docs.rs#1029)pub struct RecordBuilder<'a> {
[1030](https://docs.rs#1030)    record: Record<'a>,
[1031](https://docs.rs#1031)}
[1032](https://docs.rs#1032)

[1145](https://docs.rs#1145)/// Metadata about a log message.
[1146](https://docs.rs#1146)///
[1147](https://docs.rs#1147)/// # Use
[1148](https://docs.rs#1148)///
[1149](https://docs.rs#1149)/// `Metadata` structs are created when users of the library use
[1150](https://docs.rs#1150)/// logging macros.
[1151](https://docs.rs#1151)///
[1152](https://docs.rs#1152)/// They are consumed by implementations of the `Log` trait in the
[1153](https://docs.rs#1153)/// `enabled` method.
[1154](https://docs.rs#1154)///
[1155](https://docs.rs#1155)/// `Record`s use `Metadata` to determine the log message's severity
[1156](https://docs.rs#1156)/// and target.
[1157](https://docs.rs#1157)///
[1158](https://docs.rs#1158)/// Users should use the `log_enabled!` macro in their code to avoid
[1159](https://docs.rs#1159)/// constructing expensive log messages.
[1160](https://docs.rs#1160)///
[1161](https://docs.rs#1161)/// # Examples
[1162](https://docs.rs#1162)///
[1163](https://docs.rs#1163)/// ```
[1164](https://docs.rs#1164)/// use log::{Record, Level, Metadata};
[1165](https://docs.rs#1165)///
[1166](https://docs.rs#1166)/// struct MyLogger;
[1167](https://docs.rs#1167)///
[1168](https://docs.rs#1168)/// impl log::Log for MyLogger {
[1169](https://docs.rs#1169)///     fn enabled(&self, metadata: &Metadata) -> bool {
[1170](https://docs.rs#1170)///         metadata.level() <= Level::Info
[1171](https://docs.rs#1171)///     }
[1172](https://docs.rs#1172)///
[1173](https://docs.rs#1173)///     fn log(&self, record: &Record) {
[1174](https://docs.rs#1174)///         if self.enabled(record.metadata()) {
[1175](https://docs.rs#1175)///             println!("{} - {}", record.level(), record.args());
[1176](https://docs.rs#1176)///         }
[1177](https://docs.rs#1177)///     }
[1178](https://docs.rs#1178)///     fn flush(&self) {}
[1179](https://docs.rs#1179)/// }
[1180](https://docs.rs#1180)///
[1181](https://docs.rs#1181)/// # fn main(){}
[1182](https://docs.rs#1182)/// ```
[1183](https://docs.rs#1183)#[derive(Clone, Eq, PartialEq, Ord, PartialOrd, Hash, Debug)]
[1184](https://docs.rs#1184)pub struct Metadata<'a> {
[1185](https://docs.rs#1185)    level: Level,
[1186](https://docs.rs#1186)    target: &'a str,
[1187](https://docs.rs#1187)}
[1188](https://docs.rs#1188)
[1189](https://docs.rs#1189)impl<'a> Metadata<'a> {
[1190](https://docs.rs#1190)    /// Returns a new builder.
[1191](https://docs.rs#1191)    #[inline]
[1192](https://docs.rs#1192)    pub fn builder() -> MetadataBuilder<'a> {
[1193](https://docs.rs#1193)        MetadataBuilder::new()
[1194](https://docs.rs#1194)    }
[1195](https://docs.rs#1195)
[1196](https://docs.rs#1196)    /// The verbosity level of the message.
[1197](https://docs.rs#1197)    #[inline]
[1198](https://docs.rs#1198)    pub fn level(&self) -> Level {
[1199](https://docs.rs#1199)        self.level
[1200](https://docs.rs#1200)    }

[1209](https://docs.rs#1209)/// Builder for [`Metadata`](struct.Metadata.html).
